# SRAM Controller Behavioral Specification

## 1. Overview

The SRAM controller manages an on-chip SRAM that is protected by an always-on scrambling mechanism. It provides a bus interface for normal memory reads and writes, a separate register interface for software control and status, and a hardware interface for obtaining fresh scrambling keys. It also supports optional software-controlled initialization of the entire memory with pseudorandom data, and it enforces restrictions on executing code from SRAM.

The module must behave as a secure gateway to the SRAM: all accesses to the memory array are subject to scrambling, integrity checking, and the current security state of the controller.

## 2. Configuration and Default State

The behavior of the module is configured at elaboration time by the following parameters:

- Memory size, expressed in 32-bit words.
- Whether the execute-from-SRAM feature is present.
- Default scrambling key and nonce values.
- Default LFSR seed and permutation values.
- Whether alert signaling is asynchronous or synchronous.

Upon reset, the module must:

- Use the default scrambling key and nonce as the current key and nonce.
- Consider the default key usable for memory access.
- Have no outstanding key request.
- Clear all latched error and escalation status fields.
- Clear the key-request-complete status field.
- Clear the initialization-done status field.
- Not automatically initialize the SRAM contents.

Memory accesses may proceed immediately after reset using the default key, unless software triggers a key renewal, memory initialization, or an escalation occurs.

## 3. Scrambling Behavior

All data written to and read from the SRAM must pass through the scrambling mechanism. This includes data written during normal bus operations and during memory initialization.

The module must also scramble the address used to access the memory. Address scrambling is transparent to bus initiators.

The scrambling mechanism must always be enabled. It must not be possible for software or bus initiators to access unscrambled memory contents.

Each memory word must be stored together with its integrity-check bits. The integrity bits must be written whenever data is written and checked or returned whenever data is read. Sub-word write operations require an internal read-modify-write operation so that the integrity bits remain consistent with the full word.

## 4. Bus Interface Behavior

The module has two independent bus interfaces:

- A memory interface used to access the SRAM.
- A register interface used to access control and status registers.

The memory interface must support normal read and write transactions with byte-level write enables. Full-word writes may proceed directly. Sub-word writes must preserve the integrity bits of the surrounding word and therefore have lower throughput.

The register interface must provide software access to the control and status facilities described in this specification.

If the module is in a state where memory accesses are blocked, memory requests must be held and must not be allowed to reach the memory until the blocking condition clears. If the blocking condition is permanent, such as a latched escalation, requests remain blocked indefinitely.

## 5. Key Renewal

Software may request a new scrambling key at any time by writing to the key-renewal control field.

When a key renewal is requested, the module must:

1. Record that a key request is pending.
2. Clear the key-request-complete status field.
3. Block subsequent memory accesses until the new key is received.
4. Assert the external key request and keep it asserted until a key response is returned.

If a key request is already pending when software requests another renewal, the module must not start a second independent request. The pending request must continue until the response is received.

When the key response is accepted, the module must:

- Load the new key and nonce.
- Load the key-seed-valid indication from the response.
- Clear the pending state.
- Set the key-request-complete status field.
- Allow memory accesses to resume using the new key.

A key response may indicate that the OTP key seeds are not valid. In that case, the derived key must still be used, but the key-seed-valid status must report the invalid condition.

Renewing the key makes all previously stored memory contents unreachable, because the old key is no longer in use. Software must therefore ensure that the current SRAM contents are no longer needed before requesting a key renewal.

## 6. Memory Initialization

Software may trigger initialization of the entire SRAM with pseudorandom data.

When initialization is triggered, the module must:

1. Clear the initialization-done status field.
2. Wait until a key request has completed successfully. If software triggers initialization at the same time as a key renewal, initialization must wait until the new key and nonce are available.
3. Re-seed the pseudorandom generator using the current nonce.
4. Write pseudorandom data to every memory word.
5. Generate and write the correct integrity bits for each pseudorandom word.
6. Block normal memory accesses for the duration of the initialization sequence.
7. Set the initialization-done status field when every address has been written.

Initialization may be repeated any number of times. There is no architectural limit on the number of initialization operations.

If an initialization consistency check fails, the module must not set initialization-done. Instead, it must record an initialization error, generate a fatal alert, and enter the escalated state described below.

## 7. Instruction Fetch Control

The module may be configured to allow or disallow code execution from SRAM.

If the execute-from-SRAM feature is not present, instruction fetches from SRAM must always be denied. The related configuration inputs and register fields must have no effect.

If the execute-from-SRAM feature is present, instruction-fetch enable is controlled by an OTP-provided enable value, a life-cycle debug-enable value, and a software execute-enable field. The behavior must be:

- If the OTP enable value is in the enabled state, instruction fetches are allowed only when the software execute-enable field is also in the enabled state.
- If the OTP enable value is not in the enabled state, instruction fetches are allowed only when the life-cycle debug-enable value is in the enabled state.

Instruction fetch requests that are not allowed must be denied and must not complete as normal reads. This restriction applies only to instruction fetches; data accesses are not affected by the execute-from-SRAM policy.

## 8. Error Detection and Escalation

The module must monitor the integrity of transactions on both the memory bus interface and the register bus interface.

If an integrity error is detected on either interface, the module must:

- Record a bus-integrity-error status.
- Generate a fatal alert.
- Enter the local escalated state.

The module must also detect faults in the initialization state machine. If an initialization consistency check fails, it must:

- Record an initialization-error status.
- Generate a fatal alert.
- Enter the local escalated state.

An external escalation indication, when active, must produce the same behavior as a local escalation.

Upon entering the escalated state, the module must:

- Reset the current scrambling key and nonce to their default constants.
- Make the current scrambling context unusable so that previously stored scrambled data can no longer be read correctly.
- Block all normal memory accesses.
- Set the escalated status field.
- Clear the key-request-complete status field.
- Clear the key-seed-valid status field.
- Clear the initialization-done status field.

Once the escalated state has been entered, it must remain latched until reset. Deasserting the external escalation input must not clear the escalated state.

## 9. Alert Behavior

The module must generate a fatal alert in response to any of the following:

- A bus integrity error on either bus interface.
- An initialization consistency failure.
- A software-triggered alert test.

A software-triggered alert test must exercise the alert output path without requiring an actual error condition.

The alert output must conform to the configured alert protocol behavior for the module.

## 10. Status and Control Summary

The register interface must provide the following control functions:

- Request key renewal.
- Trigger memory initialization.
- Enable or disable instruction fetches, when the feature is present.
- Trigger an alert test.
- Protect control fields with a write-enable lock. When a control lock is active, writes to the corresponding fields must have no effect.

The register interface must provide the following status information:

- Bus-integrity-error status.
- Initialization-error status.
- Escalation status.
- Initialization-done status.
- Key-request-complete status.
- Key-seed-valid status.

Bus-integrity-error, initialization-error, and escalation statuses, once set, must remain set until reset. The key-request-complete status is cleared when a key request starts or when escalation occurs, and is set when a key response is accepted. The initialization-done status is cleared when a new initialization starts or when escalation occurs, and is set when initialization completes.

The key and nonce values themselves must never be readable by software.
